comparator.name: Literary Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The official 2026-2027 OER fixes a 180-EC bachelor: a 120-EC major and 60-EC profiling space. The major contains 75 EC of compulsory study, including eight 7.5-EC foundational courses, Literary Toolbox, Republic of Letters and the bachelor thesis; a 30-EC depth package; and one 7.5-EC context elective. The generic normalized target does not choose between the two depth packages. Literature Across Borders is selected by official order, independently of UCR fit, and its four published courses are reconstructed. Retorica is likewise selected as the first published context elective. The profiling space remains open rather than being filled for UCR convenience.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized Literary Studies target does not select between the two formal 30-EC depth packages. The current official programme page and 2026-2027 OER list Literature Across Borders before Literature in Conflict, so it is selected by official order before considering UCR fit. Retorica is selected on the same basis as the first published context elective; the 60-EC profiling space remains open.

selection.assessment: The closest match owns the target’s general literary interpretation, literary history, literature-and-society and narrative-form interests. Both separately documented depth directions generate coherent, feasible and materially distinct UCR pathways: Literature across Borders and Literature in Conflict. Their schedules differ pairwise by seven to fourteen courses and pass the hard constraints, so the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

alternatives.label: Literary Studies, History & Cultural Analysis
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum integrates literary close reading and theory with art history, film and media, cultural memory, philosophy, sociology and qualitative and historical research.
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response combines sustained literary interpretation and theory with literary and cultural history, film and media, cultural criticism, social context and qualitative humanities research.
progression: Introductory literature, media, art history, history and sociology precede advanced literary meaning, film-and-text, cultural theory, media and race, social theory and research. Every course is offered in its assigned semester and the pathway builds from interpretation and historical context toward advanced criticism and independent inquiry.

alternatives.label: Comparative Literature, Media & Transnational Culture
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum forms a clear sequence in literature, film, media, rhetoric and creative communication, complemented by art history, archaeology, philosophy and qualitative research.
alternatives.concept: A Literature across Borders pathway connecting world literature, life and travel writing, adaptation, media, rhetoric and cultural communication with postcolonial, historical and philosophical contexts.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest match, this pathway replaces broad sociology, social theory, historical research and some art-history coverage with rhetoric, material culture, environmental media, philosophy and advanced cultural communication. Seven of the 24 courses differ, and the organising emphasis is how literature and cultural forms travel across borders and media.
progression: Introductions to literature, media and rhetoric precede advanced life writing, film-and-text, literary meaning, media-and-race and cultural-communication work. Historical, archaeological, philosophical and qualitative foundations support comparative and transnational interpretation; all courses are offered in their assigned semesters.

alternatives.label: Literature, Conflict & Cultural Power
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum studies culture through history, political thought, sociology, media, literature, heritage and social movements, with sustained attention to inequality, identity and power.
alternatives.concept: A Literature in Conflict pathway organised around identity, colonialism, inequality, dissent and political power across literature, media, history, philosophy, art and heritage.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest match, this pathway replaces most art-history, literary-analysis and creative-communication study with political philosophy, comparative and international politics, empire, gender history, social movements, heritage and conflict. Fourteen of the 24 courses differ, and literature is situated within explicit questions of identity, dissent and power.
progression: Foundations in history, political philosophy, sociology, gender, ethics, comparative politics, media and literature precede advanced social theory, European politics, media and race, heritage, conflict and historical research. Every course is offered in its assigned semester; there are no unmet formal prerequisites.

blocks: Both place early-modern cultural production in European and wider connected contexts; UCR focuses on visual art rather than literature.
Both prepare advanced humanities inquiry through source-based research, critical positioning and sustained academic writing; UCR is art-historical.
Both introduce literary studies, close reading and foundational concepts of textual interpretation.
UCR studies major works across historical periods, including classical and medieval traditions, covering a substantial part of this literary-history component.
Both analyse how close attention to style, rhetoric and formal choices produces meaning; UCR concentrates on language and style.
Both examine twentieth-century to contemporary cultural forms and changing media; UCR focuses on media history rather than literary history.
Both examine mobility, place, identity and intercultural encounter through life and travel narratives.
Both analyse representation, race, identity and power through postcolonial and critical frameworks; UCR focuses on media.
Both develop advanced critical interpretation and examine competing theories of literary and cultural meaning.
Both apply critical cultural analysis to ecological questions; UCR focuses on visual and audiovisual environmental media.
Both engage advanced contemporary critical debates about culture, identity, institutions and social change; UCR approaches them through social theory.
Both study modern European cultural and social transformations over the long nineteenth century; UCR is general history rather than literary history.
Both develop rhetorical analysis, argument, writing and presentation.
Both develop qualitative research design, interpretation and reflexive analysis, though UCR is broader social research rather than a literary-methods course.

notes.text: Utrecht requires a complete four-period literary-history sequence, dedicated literary methods, a selected 30-EC depth package, thesis preparation and a bachelor thesis. UCR can build strong combinations in literary interpretation, world literature, life writing, film and media, cultural history, philosophy, sociology, politics and qualitative research, but offers fewer dedicated literature courses, no equivalent complete period sequence or depth package, and no compulsory bachelor thesis; the standardised Optional independent research element remains optional.
